newsitem.title: USA: Senate opens debate on controversial amendment.
newsitem.headline: Senate opens debate on controversial amendment.

text.p: The Senate Wednesday opened debate on the Republican-backed balanced budget amendment to the Constitution as the White House pressured wavering Democrats to reject it.

The House and Senate were expected to vote at the end of the month in what will be a key test for Republicans who made passage of the historic amendment their legislative priority for the year. They lost by the narrowest of margins in 1995 when it passed the House and failed by one vote in the Senate.

Several Democrats were expected to offer alternatives but the most worrisome to Republicans was one that would address President Clinton's complaint that Social Security would be harmed if kept under the balanced budget umbrella.
Republicans were concerned that a vote for this alternative would give Democrats political cover while creating a loophole so large the balanced budget amendment would be ineffective.

With a digital clock flashing an $8,000 per second increase in the national debt, Republican and Democratic supporters from the House and Senate argued at a news conference that Washington needed the discipline of a constitutional amendment to bring the federal deficit to zero.
"We need to have the balanced budget amendment as an insurance policy," said House Budget Committee chairman John Kasich, Republican of Ohio.

"A balanced budget amendment will bring about the fiscal discipline our country so desperately needs," Sen. Richard Bryan of Nevada, one of the seven Democrats pledged to vote for it, said during the opening debate.
Sen. Edward Kennedy of Massachusetts, one of the most outspoken opponents, argued it would be bad policy.
"It is unnecessary, unwise and untimely. At the very moment when Congress is preparing to balance the budget the right way, our Republican friends are proposing to do it the wrong way," he said.

A constitutional amendment to require a balanced budget during peacetime has been under debate since 1989. It would make it more difficult for Congress to raise taxes, approve deficit spending or increase the public debt.
Even as they pledged bipartisanship to balance the budget by 2002 Republicans jeered Clinton who during his State of the Union address Tuesday urged them to reject the balanced budget amendment.

Though he once said he did not object, Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin convinced him otherwise and said tying the government's fiscal policy to the Constitution would turn economic recessions into depressions.
Republican senators were united and their best chance of victory was division within the Democrats where seven agreed to support the amendment.

All eyes were on four freshmen Democrats who made campaign pledges to vote for it, but did not commit to vote for the Republican version and raised concerns it would harm Social Security. The amendment would have to get 67 votes to pass.

In the House, support grew even among Republicans for an exemption for Social Security. House Judiciary Committee chariman Henry Hyde, Republican of Illinois, abruptly postponed Wednesday's vote on a Democratic change to exempt Social Security when it appeared Republicans would not arrive in time to defeat it. House Speaker Newt Gingrich said the issue will be addressed with a resolution to protect Social Security trust funds.
It would have to get 289 of 435 House votes to pass and then would go to the states where in the next seven years it would have to be ratified by 38 of 50 states to become the 28th amendment.
